principle_name: The Trust Equation — Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy Divided by Self-Orientation
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: As the diagnostic framework for any stalled or struggling MOTM client or prospect relationship. When a BD person is not getting traction, map the relationship against all four components to identify which dimension is the problem — not just assume it is credibility.
when_not_to_use: Do not use the equation mechanically or as a checklist to run through in a BD conversation. It is a diagnostic tool for the BD person, not a script for the client.
principle: Trust has four components. Credibility is whether the client believes what you say and respects your expertise. Reliability is whether the client believes you do what you say you will do, consistently. Intimacy is whether the client feels safe discussing sensitive, difficult, or personal issues with you. Self-Orientation is the degree to which the client perceives that you are focused on yourself rather than on them. Credibility and Reliability are in the numerator — they add to trust. Self-Orientation is in the denominator — it divides trust. Even a professional with high credibility and reliability will be distrusted if their self-orientation is perceived to be high. The highest leverage for improving trust is almost always reducing self-orientation — the factor most professionals neglect because they believe credibility is all that matters.
questions_to_ask: Of these four factors — credibility, reliability, intimacy, self-orientation — which one is most limiting this relationship right now?
Does this client perceive me as being primarily focused on helping them — or on winning the engagement and advancing MOTM's commercial interests?
Have I created enough moments where this client felt comfortable sharing something difficult or sensitive with me?
recommended_action: For any important MOTM client or prospect relationship, score each of the four trust equation components from 1-10. Identify the weakest component and address it directly. If self-orientation is high in the client's perception, the most important action is to do things that demonstrably put their interests ahead of MOTM's commercial interest — even at short-term cost to MOTM.
what_not_to_do: Do not assume that technical credibility is sufficient for trust. Do not focus all BD effort on demonstrating expertise while ignoring reliability, intimacy, and self-orientation. Do not mistake the absence of distrust for the presence of trust — they are different states.
motm_application: A MOTM BD person who has high credibility (the client knows MOTM can execute) and reasonable reliability (MOTM delivers on commitments) but low intimacy (the client never shares the real challenges, only the sanitised version) and high perceived self-orientation (every conversation leads back to expanding MOTM's scope) will not build a trusted advisor relationship. The fix is to reduce self-orientation — to have conversations where MOTM visibly prioritises the client's interests over its own.

principle_name: Self-Orientation Is the Denominator — It Destroys More Trust Than Anything Else
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: Every time there is a temptation to steer the conversation toward MOTM's services before fully understanding the client's situation. High self-orientation is the single most common reason sophisticated buyers disengage from BD conversations.
when_not_to_use: Reducing self-orientation does not mean never asking for business or never proposing MOTM's services. It means ensuring that every action the client observes is visibly in their interest — and that the ask comes after the value is established.
principle: Self-orientation is in the denominator of the trust equation because it multiplies the negative effect of every other factor. A client who perceives that the advisor is primarily interested in winning business, advancing their own agenda, or looking impressive will discount every other positive signal — no matter how credible, reliable, or intimate the relationship is. Self-orientation manifests in many ways that advisors do not recognise: relating stories back to yourself, giving answers too quickly, filling silences with solutions, name-dropping, presenting credentials unprompted, wanting to be seen as adding value more than actually adding value. The only antidote is genuinely shifting focus to the client — not as a technique, but as a sincere orientation.
questions_to_ask: In our last conversation with this client, how much of the time were we talking about MOTM versus talking about their situation?
What is the one thing I could do for this client this week that would visibly put their interests ahead of MOTM's commercial interests?
If this client described our relationship to a colleague, would they say we are one of the few advisors who genuinely focuses on their problems?
recommended_action: Before every MOTM client or prospect meeting, write down the one thing the client most needs from this meeting — not from MOTM's perspective, but from theirs. Start every meeting by asking what would make this the most valuable conversation possible for them. Resist the temptation to fill silences with solutions or to redirect conversations toward MOTM's capabilities.
what_not_to_do: Do not open BD meetings by presenting MOTM's capabilities or case studies unless the client has specifically asked. Do not relate the client's problems to similar work MOTM has done for other clients before demonstrating you understand this client's specific situation. Do not jump to solutions before the client has finished describing their problem.
motm_application: When a MOTM BD person meets a prospect MD for the first time, the instinct is to demonstrate what MOTM can do. The trusted advisor approach is the opposite: ask questions that demonstrate genuine understanding of the MD's specific situation, listen without redirecting to MOTM's solutions, and offer a perspective that is helpful to the MD regardless of whether it leads to a MOTM engagement. The MD who experiences this will trust MOTM more than any competitor who led with a capability presentation.

principle_name: The Trusted Advisor Pyramid — From Vendor to Trusted Advisor Is a Four-Stage Evolution
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
chapter: Chapter 2 — What Is a Trusted Advisor?
when_to_use: When diagnosing where MOTM currently sits in any given client relationship, and determining what it would take to move to a higher level. Also useful in framing how MOTM positions itself in BD conversations — not as a vendor of sales execution services, but as a strategic partner.
when_not_to_use: Not all clients need or want a trusted advisor relationship — some want a well-executed vendor. Do not force the relationship to a higher level than the client is ready for or wants.
principle: Client-advisor relationships evolve through four levels. Level 1: Service-Based — the advisor delivers a specific technical task with excellence. Level 2: Needs-Based — the advisor solves broader problems, not just the initial task. Level 3: Valuable Resource — the advisor offers perspective and context across strategic issues related to their expertise. Level 4: Trusted Advisor — virtually all issues, personal and professional, are open to discussion. The trusted advisor is the person the client calls first when a significant issue arises. The critical insight is that the pyramid is defined by two dimensions: breadth of issues and depth of personal relationship. Moving up requires both. A relationship with broad issue coverage but shallow personal depth remains at Level 3. A relationship with deep personal trust but narrow issue scope is also Level 3. Only the combination of both produces a trusted advisor.
questions_to_ask: At what level of the pyramid does our most important MOTM client currently see us — and is that the level we want to be at?
What would it take for this client to start calling MOTM first when a sales challenge arises — before calling any other advisor?
Are we too narrowly defined by what we were initially hired to do, limiting our ability to move up the pyramid?
recommended_action: For every major MOTM client, identify their current pyramid level and map the path to moving one level higher. The path almost always requires: demonstrating expertise beyond the initial scope, building deeper personal relationship with the primary buyer, and proactively engaging on broader business issues beyond the immediate sales execution mandate.
what_not_to_do: Do not assume that excellent delivery at Level 1 or 2 will automatically produce progression to Level 3 or 4. Do not allow MOTM to be permanently defined by the client only in terms of the initial service scope. Do not expect the pyramid level to rise without actively investing in the relationship dimensions.
motm_application: Most MOTM engagements start at Level 1 — a specific sales execution mandate. The goal should be to move to Level 3 (Valuable Resource) within the first 6 months, and toward Level 4 (Trusted Advisor) over 12-18 months with the right clients. The BD person's task is to expand the conversation beyond execution metrics to include strategic sales questions the client has not yet thought to ask MOTM.

principle_name: Trust Must Be Earned — Go First, Give Before You Ask, Demonstrate Before You Assert
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
chapter: Chapter 3 — Earning Trust & Chapter 5 — Rules of Romance
when_to_use: In every initial engagement with a new prospect, and in expanding any existing relationship to a new buyer. Trust must be earned before it is leveraged — and the person seeking the relationship must go first.
when_not_to_use: Do not use giving as a manipulation tactic. If the giving is not genuine — if it is really a technique to extract something in return — prospects will detect it and the effect will be the opposite of trust.
principle: The key to earning trust is to give before you receive. The lawyer who provided free, comprehensive information about probating a will before being retained — including information that had nothing to do with the lawyer's fees — won the business because he demonstrated genuine commitment to the client's interests. The dentist who called every evening to check on patients earned trust through small, consistent acts of caring. The principle is: Go First. You must invest in the relationship before expecting a return. Illustrate, don't tell. Demonstrate that you understand, have done your homework, and care about this specific person's situation — do not assert it. Earning trust requires personal risk and generosity. The professional who says trust me earns none; the professional who gives without expectation earns it rapidly.
questions_to_ask: What is one thing I could do for this prospect before our first meeting that would demonstrate genuine investment in their situation?
Am I waiting for the client to demonstrate they value the relationship before I invest in it — or am I willing to go first?
What can MOTM offer this prospect that is genuinely valuable to them, independent of whether it leads to an engagement?
recommended_action: Before any first meeting with a prospect, do substantive research on their specific situation and prepare two or three observations that are genuinely useful to them — not generic MOTM content. Offer something of value in the first interaction that has no strings attached. This could be a relevant insight about their industry, a connection to someone useful, or a specific perspective on a challenge they face.
what_not_to_do: Do not open a first meeting with a MOTM capability presentation — this signals that the purpose of the meeting is to sell, not to help. Do not claim you understand the client's situation before demonstrating it through specific, accurate observations. Do not expect the client to trust MOTM before MOTM has given them a reason to.
motm_application: When approaching a new prospect, a MOTM BD person should invest meaningful time understanding that specific company's commercial situation before making first contact. The outreach should lead with an observation specific to that company — something that demonstrates MOTM has thought about their situation — not with a description of MOTM's services. The first call should give something useful before asking for anything. This is how the Maister lawyer won the probate business: by giving first.

principle_name: Intimacy Is the Scarcest and Most Powerful Trust Factor — Create Safety for Difficult Conversations
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: Whenever a client relationship feels surface-level — where the client only shares the sanitised version of their challenges and never reveals the real problems, political dynamics, or personal concerns. Intimacy is the factor that unlocks the real advisory relationship.
when_not_to_use: Do not rush intimacy by raising personal or sensitive topics before the relationship has the foundation to support it. Premature intimacy attempts backfire. The dance must be gradual and mutual.
principle: Intimacy is about emotional closeness around the issues at hand — not about personal friendship. A client who will talk freely about the real challenges, the political dynamics, the personal fears, and the genuine uncertainties is in an intimate advisory relationship. This is the rarest form of trust because it requires both parties to take personal risks. Greater intimacy means fewer topics are off limits. The key insight is that intimacy is a dance: one party offers something personal and the other either responds (deepening intimacy) or does not (drawing a line). The advisor must almost always take the first step — and must do so with appropriate phrasing that gives the client an easy exit if they are not ready. The risk of being too careful about intimacy is that conversations remain permanently surface-level, which means the advisor can never help with what actually matters.
questions_to_ask: Does this client share the real situation with me — or the version they would share with any vendor?
What topic has this client been hinting at but never raised directly — and do I have the courage to name it?
Am I holding back from going deeper in this relationship because I am afraid of how it will be received?
recommended_action: Identify one topic in each key client relationship that both parties are aware of but have not yet discussed directly. Practice the naming and claiming technique: acknowledge that the topic is difficult to raise, accept responsibility for raising it, and then state it directly. Give the client an easy way to decline engagement with the topic. In most cases, the client will be relieved that someone finally named it.
what_not_to_do: Do not maintain professional distance as a virtue — emotional closeness around the issues at hand is a professional requirement, not a boundary violation. Do not wait for the client to take the first intimacy step — they are unlikely to do so. Do not raise intensely personal topics too early in a relationship before any trust foundation exists.
motm_application: A MOTM BD person who always has professional, positive meetings with a client but never learns about the real internal dynamics — the MD who is frustrated with the Sales Head, the commercial strategy debate between divisions, the board pressure on growth targets — is operating at the surface. The trusted advisor relationship requires the courage to say: it sounds like there is something more going on here — and I want to make sure I understand your real situation, not just the formal version. This creates the depth that produces genuine advisory trust.

principle_name: How to Give Advice — Earn the Right Before You Offer the Answer
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: Every time a MOTM BD person is tempted to jump to recommending a solution before fully demonstrating that they understand the client's specific situation. Advice given before the right is earned will be rejected — even if it is correct.
when_not_to_use: When a client explicitly asks for a direct recommendation, deliver it directly. Some clients do not want the Socratic process — they want the answer. Match the approach to the individual client.
principle: Advice giving is not a logical exercise — it is an emotional duet. Being right is not sufficient; the advisor must also earn the right to be heard. Earning the right has three parts: understanding the client's situation, understanding how the client feels about it, and convincing the client that you understand both. The advisor who jumps immediately to the answer — even when correct — signals that they are more interested in demonstrating their expertise than in understanding the client. The Socratic approach — leading the client through a series of questions that help them see the answer — produces far more durable commitment because the client experiences the insight as their own. The teacher analogy is exact: the advisor's job is to help the client get from where they are (their current understanding) to where they need to be, step by step, not to announce the destination.
questions_to_ask: Have I understood this client's situation well enough to have earned the right to offer a recommendation?
What does this client feel about their current situation — not just what do they know about it?
Am I giving advice that the client is ready to hear — or advice that I am ready to give?
recommended_action: Before offering any recommendation in a MOTM BD or delivery conversation, demonstrate understanding of the client's specific situation through specific, accurate observations. Ask the client to confirm that your understanding is correct. Only then introduce a recommendation — and frame it as an option to consider, not an answer to accept. Use the four-step process: give them their options, educate them about the options, give your recommendation, and let them choose.
what_not_to_do: Do not lead with the answer before demonstrating understanding of the question. Do not present MOTM's recommended approach as the obvious solution before the client has confirmed that you understand their specific situation. Do not interpret client silence or politeness as acceptance of your recommendation — ask directly whether your recommendation makes sense for their situation.
motm_application: When a MOTM BD person diagnoses a client's sales execution problem and immediately recommends a specific SE structure, they may be right — but the client will not commit unless they feel understood first. The better approach: describe what you are observing about their sales situation, ask the client whether that matches their experience, explore why the current situation exists, help them see the implications of continuing as-is, and only then recommend the MOTM approach. The recommendation lands differently when the client has already acknowledged the problem.

principle_name: The Five-Stage Trust Building Process — Engage, Listen, Frame, Envision, Commit
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: As the structural framework for every substantive BD or advisory conversation with a MOTM client or prospect. The five stages provide the sequence for building trust in a single conversation or across an extended relationship.
when_not_to_use: Do not rigidly apply the five stages as a formal process in every conversation. They are a guideline for the sequence of trust-building, not a script. The most common error is skipping stages — especially Framing and Envisioning — to get to Commitment faster.
principle: Trust develops through five stages. Engage: the client believes there is an issue worth discussing and this advisor is worth discussing it with. Listen: the client comes to believe the advisor genuinely understands them. Frame: the advisor helps the client crystallise and clarify the real nature of their problem — not just the presenting issue. Envision: the advisor and client jointly imagine what the desired future state looks like in specific, concrete terms. Commit: the advisor ensures the client understands what it will actually take to achieve the vision and has the genuine will to do it. The most common failure is jumping from Engage directly to Commit — skipping Listen, Frame, and Envision entirely. This produces advisory relationships that feel transactional, commitments that do not hold, and clients who do not feel genuinely understood.
questions_to_ask: Has this client genuinely come to believe that I understand their situation — or have I moved to the solution too quickly?
Have we jointly articulated a clear picture of what the desired future state looks like — in their terms, not MOTM's?
Does this client understand what it will actually take to achieve what we have described — and are they committed to doing it?
recommended_action: Map each important MOTM BD conversation against the five stages. Identify which stage is weakest and invest in it before moving forward. If the conversation keeps stalling at Commitment, it is almost always because Listen or Frame was not done adequately — the client does not feel understood or has not crystallised their own problem clearly enough to commit to solving it.
what_not_to_do: Do not skip Framing — clarifying the real nature of the problem — in order to get to the solution faster. Do not skip Envisioning — the concrete picture of the desired future state — because it feels abstract or slow. These two stages are where the greatest trust-building occurs and where the advisor most clearly adds value that distinguishes them from a vendor.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect says they need to think about it after a proposal meeting, the issue is almost always that one of the five stages was incomplete. The most common gap is Framing — the client has not crystallised their problem clearly enough to feel urgency to solve it — or Envisioning — they have not developed a vivid, specific picture of what success would look like. The fix is to go back one stage, not to push harder on Commitment.

principle_name: Engagement — Get the Client to Open Up Before Anything Else Can Happen
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: When a prospect is not engaging with MOTM's outreach — when calls are not returned, meetings are agreed to but remain surface-level, or when an existing client has become unreachable. Engagement is the prerequisite for everything else.
when_not_to_use: Engagement techniques that feel like gimmicks or manufactured interest will damage rather than build trust. Every engagement approach must be rooted in genuine relevance to the specific client's situation.
principle: Engagement requires two things simultaneously: the client must believe there is an issue worth talking about, and that this particular advisor is worth talking to about it. Most BD efforts fail at engagement not because the prospect is uninterested, but because the advisor has not demonstrated that they are genuinely worth talking to. The CFO who told partners that too many advisors come in just asking about his problems and bringing nothing — is describing the failure of engagement. Something valuable must be brought to every meeting — a genuine insight, a relevant observation, a specific piece of analysis — before the client will open up. For existing clients, re-engagement requires something new, intriguing, or fresh that gives the client a reason to open up on a new issue.
questions_to_ask: What specific, valuable insight can I bring to this meeting that this client has not already heard from every other advisor?
Have I given this prospect a compelling reason to invest their time in talking to me specifically — not just to any advisor?
For existing clients who have gone quiet, what new observation or fresh perspective might re-open the conversation?
recommended_action: Before any first meeting or re-engagement with a dormant client, prepare a specific observation about their competitive situation, market position, or sales execution that is genuinely useful and somewhat unexpected. Approach them by offering to share insights that are relevant to their specific situation — not to sell MOTM's services. The observation should be valuable regardless of whether they engage MOTM.
what_not_to_do: Do not approach a first meeting asking the client to describe their problems — as the CFO in the book said, this brings no value. Do not offer generic MOTM content as engagement bait — it must be specific to this client's situation. Do not confuse being accepted into a meeting with being genuinely engaged — the client may be polite without being open.
motm_application: A MOTM first meeting that opens with a presentation of MOTM's services and asks the MD to describe their challenges will not create genuine engagement. A meeting that opens with: We have spent time studying your commercial situation and we noticed something that might be important — is the difference between a vendor meeting and a trusted advisor conversation. The observation must be specific, accurate, and genuinely relevant to the MD's current situation.

principle_name: The Art of Listening — Trust Cannot Be Built Without Being Perceived to Listen
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: In every MOTM BD and client conversation. Listening is the most consistently underperformed trust-building skill among professionals who believe their expertise is their primary value.
when_not_to_use: This is a permanent discipline — there is no conversation in which active, empathetic listening is not appropriate. The only variation is the depth of the emotional listening required, which increases with the stakes of the topic being discussed.
principle: Jack Welch said the advisor he most valued listened better than anyone else. This is not accidental. Listening is the second stage of the five-stage trust process and it is the prerequisite for everything that follows. Good listening must be active — it is not passive absorption of information. It requires: listening for what is said and what is unspoken, confirming and validating what has been heard, acknowledging the emotional dimension of what the client is sharing, and making the client experience being genuinely heard. Most professionals listen too rationally — hearing the logical content of what is said without acknowledging the feelings behind it. A client who says we process 300,000 transactions a day is also communicating pride, or anxiety, or exhaustion — and the advisor who responds only to the number misses what matters most.
questions_to_ask: What is the emotion behind what this client is telling me — not just the content?
Have I given this client the experience of genuinely being heard — or have I moved too quickly to my response?
What has this client been hinting at but not yet said directly?
recommended_action: In every MOTM client conversation, identify the emotional dimension of what the client is sharing and acknowledge it explicitly before responding to the content. Practice the three-stage listening sequence: reflective listening (I hear you saying…), supportive listening (that must be difficult…), and listening for possibility (what have you considered doing about this?). Do not interrupt, do not fill silences with solutions, and do not redirect the client to MOTM's agenda before they have finished expressing their own.
what_not_to_do: Do not listen only for the parts of the client's story that are relevant to MOTM's services. Do not interrupt to show that you understand — let the client finish their thought. Do not give solutions before the client has had the full experience of being heard. Do not ask closed questions that confirm your existing hypothesis before you have heard the client's version.
motm_application: In a MOTM discovery conversation, if the MD mentions that their Sales Head is struggling with a particular challenge, the trusted advisor instinct is to listen for what is really being said — is this frustration? Anxiety about a key hire? A signal of a deeper commercial problem? And then to acknowledge that dimension: it sounds like this has been difficult to navigate. That one sentence, delivered with genuine attention, opens the conversation far wider than any clever question about MOTM's services.

principle_name: Framing the Issue — Redefining the Problem Is Often More Valuable Than Solving It
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: When a client has described their problem in a way that is unclear, blame-laden, self-oriented, or focused on symptoms rather than causes. The trusted advisor reframes the problem so that it can actually be addressed — this is often the highest-value contribution of the whole conversation.
when_not_to_use: Do not reframe a problem that the client has defined clearly and accurately — adding complexity where none exists is not helpful. Apply framing when the client's definition of the problem is blocking progress.
principle: Framing is the act of crystallising the client's complex issues into a problem definition that provides insight and a fresh way of thinking. An accurate problem statement is often more than halfway to the solution. There are two types of framing. Rational framing: distilling a complex situation to a few critical variables that clarify what is really happening. Emotional framing: surfacing the hidden emotional or political dynamics that everyone knows are present but no one has named. Emotional framing requires the courage to say what has not been said — to name the elephant in the room. The naming and claiming technique makes this manageable: acknowledge the difficulty of raising the issue, accept responsibility for raising it, and then state it directly. Most initial client problem statements are loaded with blame and are too close to the symptom to be actionable. The trusted advisor helps the client move from blame to responsibility in describing the problem.
questions_to_ask: Is the client describing the real problem — or a symptom, or a blame-laden version of the problem?
What is the elephant in the room that everyone is aware of but no one has named?
How would I describe this situation if I removed all the blame from the problem statement?
recommended_action: When a client describes their commercial problem, listen for blame (they won't listen, the team doesn't follow through, the market is difficult) and reframe it into an actionable, blame-free problem definition. Use naming and claiming to raise the hidden emotional dynamic when it is present. Offer the reframed problem statement as a hypothesis and invite the client to refine it.
what_not_to_do: Do not accept the client's initial problem statement as the final definition — most initial statements are symptomatic, blame-laden, or self-protective. Do not avoid emotional framing because it feels risky — the risk of leaving the elephant unnamed is greater than the risk of naming it carefully. Do not frame the problem in MOTM's terms before understanding it in the client's terms.
motm_application: If a client MD says the problem is that my Sales Head is not performing, the trusted advisor response is not to immediately pitch MOTM as a replacement. It is to explore what is really happening: is this a skills gap, a resource gap, a strategic misalignment, a communication problem between the MD and the Sales Head? Helping the MD reframe the problem accurately is the highest-value action MOTM can take — and it earns far more trust than any service proposal.

principle_name: Envisioning — Help the Client Paint a Concrete Picture of the Desired Future
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: After framing the problem clearly, before proposing any solution. When a client intellectually accepts that there is a problem but does not feel urgency to address it — they have not yet visualised what success would actually look like.
when_not_to_use: Do not use abstract envisioning language when the client needs concrete specifics. The vision must be tangible enough that the client can feel it, not just understand it conceptually.
principle: Envisioning is the most often neglected stage of trust building. After a problem has been framed clearly, the natural instinct — for both advisor and client — is to jump immediately to action. But action without a concrete vision produces weak commitment and poor follow-through. The envisioning stage asks: what are we really aiming for? What will it look like when we get there? How will we know we are there? When done well, envisioning transforms an abstract problem into a specific, desirable future state that energises commitment. The language of envisioning is the language of possibility: wouldn't it be great if…, imagine what it would look like when…, how would things be different if…. Envisioning makes the solution feel real and achievable before the difficult work of getting there begins.
questions_to_ask: Can you describe specifically what your commercial situation would look like in 12 months if this problem were fully solved?
What would you be doing differently — and what would your team be doing differently — in that future state?
How would you know that the engagement had been successful?
recommended_action: Before presenting the MOTM proposal, invest time in envisioning the client's desired future state in specific, concrete terms. Ask questions that help the client paint a vivid picture of what success looks like — in their language, about their specific situation. Only after the future state is concrete and compelling does the commitment to pursuing it become durable.
what_not_to_do: Do not skip envisioning in order to get to the proposal faster — this is the most common cause of proposals that get accepted in principle but never implemented. Do not envision in MOTM's terms (what MOTM will deliver) before envisioning in the client's terms (what they want to achieve). Do not allow the envisioning conversation to remain abstract — push for specificity.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect says the right things in a discovery meeting but the proposal stalls, the issue is almost always that envisioning was skipped. The client intellectually accepted the problem but never emotionally connected with the solution. The fix is to go back to envisioning: can we take a moment to describe exactly what your commercial situation would look like in 12 months if this worked as well as we believe it can? This conversation reactivates the emotional motivation that the proposal process had drained away.

principle_name: Commitment — Ensure the Client Understands the Real Cost of the Journey Before They Start
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: Before closing any MOTM engagement. True commitment requires that the client understands not just the benefit of the engagement but the effort, risk, internal change, and personal investment that it will require of them.
when_not_to_use: Do not use commitment conversations to frighten clients out of engaging. The purpose is to produce durable commitment by ensuring the client has realistic expectations — not to lower the probability of conversion.
principle: Commitment in the trusted advisor context is not just the agreement to proceed — it is the emotional state of being truly ready and willing to do what it takes. The commitment stage is where the advisor plays devil's advocate: let me try to convince you not to do this, so that you enter the engagement knowing what you are actually committing to. Advisors who skip commitment in order to close faster produce clients who are committed in principle but not in practice — who run into the first difficulty and disengage. The most trust-building thing an advisor can do at commitment is to be completely candid about the challenges, risks, and requirements. A client who hears the advisor raise the difficulties before they do will trust the advisor far more than one who hears only optimistic promises. Managing expectations: always tell the exact truth about what you can and cannot do, and when you can and cannot deliver.
questions_to_ask: What are the biggest internal obstacles to this engagement producing the results we have been discussing — and is the client aware of them?
Is this client genuinely committed to doing what it will take — or are they committed to the idea of it?
What might go wrong in the first 90 days of this engagement, and has the client agreed on how they will respond?
recommended_action: Before closing any MOTM engagement, have an explicit commitment conversation that covers: what MOTM will do and will not do, what the client will need to do and may find difficult, what could go wrong and how both parties will respond, and how success will be measured. Raise the risks and challenges before the client does. This earns more trust than any promise of easy success.
what_not_to_do: Do not project false confidence that everything will go smoothly in order to close the engagement. Do not skip the explicit discussion of what the client must contribute internally for the engagement to work. Do not accept verbal commitment without exploring whether the client has the internal will and support to follow through.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect agrees to engage, the trusted advisor approach is to say: before we sign anything, I want to make sure we are both clear on what this will require. There will be moments in the first 60 days where your internal team may resist the new sales structure. There will be a period before the pipeline starts to build where it may not feel like it is working. Are you genuinely prepared to push through that period — and is your team aligned? This conversation produces engagements that survive the inevitable difficult early period.

principle_name: Naming and Claiming — Surface the Unspeakable with Courage and Care
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: Whenever something important is clearly present in a conversation but neither party is naming it — when there is an elephant in the room, a topic everyone is aware of but no one will raise. The naming and claiming technique is the tool for addressing this without creating defensiveness.
when_not_to_use: Do not use naming and claiming to raise topics that are genuinely private or none of the advisor's business. The technique applies to issues that are relevant to the matter at hand but are being avoided for emotional or political reasons.
principle: Naming and claiming is characterized by three elements: an acknowledgment of the difficulty of raising the issue, acceptance of personal responsibility for raising it, and a direct statement of the issue itself. The technique works because it takes the risk of naming something uncomfortable onto the advisor — the client does not have to bear the vulnerability of raising it first. The list of responsibility-taking caveats (I'm probably the only one who noticed this, but… / I'm not sure if this is appropriate to raise, but…) provides the scaffolding for surfacing difficult truths. The Columbo technique — appearing to be confused, uncertain, or out of one's depth while being highly perceptive — is a sophisticated application of the same principle. A client who experiences an advisor naming something real and difficult, with courage and care, will trust that advisor at a depth that no credential or case study can achieve.
questions_to_ask: What is the thing in this relationship or this conversation that everyone is aware of but no one is saying?
If I named that thing directly, what is the worst realistic outcome — and is it actually worse than not naming it?
What responsibility-taking caveat would make it easier for me to raise this without putting the client on the defensive?
recommended_action: Before any important MOTM BD or delivery meeting, identify the one thing that is most important and least likely to be discussed without prompting. Prepare to name it using the responsibility-taking caveat approach. Practice the phrasing in advance. After naming the issue, pause and let the client respond — do not immediately offer a solution.
what_not_to_do: Do not avoid naming difficult realities because they feel too personal or too risky. The risk of not naming important things is consistently greater than the risk of naming them carefully. Do not name something difficult and then immediately offer a solution — the value is in naming it and creating space for the client to respond. Do not name something real with the wrong tone — it must feel like courage, not criticism.
motm_application: If a MOTM client's Sales Head has been resisting the MOTM SE's approach for three months, the trusted advisor conversation is not to keep reporting progress metrics. It is to say: I want to raise something directly. I am seeing some friction between our SE and your Sales Head around how new accounts are being prioritised. I may have this wrong, but it feels like it is affecting results in a way that we should address openly. Do you see it the same way? This naming creates the conversation that had been avoided — and usually accelerates the resolution dramatically.

principle_name: Trust Is Personal — Institutional Trust Does Not Exist; Only Individual Trust Does
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
when_to_use: In every MOTM BD conversation and client relationship. The implication for MOTM is profound: no amount of MOTM brand, methodology, or case studies can substitute for the trust that individual MOTM people must build with individual clients.
when_not_to_use: This is not an argument against having a strong MOTM brand — institutional reputation can get MOTM onto a prospect's short list. But it cannot close the engagement or retain the client. Only individual human trust can do that.
principle: Institutional trust is an oxymoron. People trust people, not organisations. Brand recognition and reputation may get a firm considered, but only a person can make a client feel understood, respected, and cared for. The Texaco advertisement — you can trust your car to the man who wears the star — was more honest than it intended: it was still the man they were trusting, not the star. The implications for MOTM are profound: the BD person who meets a prospect is building personal trust, not corporate trust. The SE who is embedded with a client is building personal trust, not MOTM trust. When that person leaves, the trust does not automatically transfer to their replacement. Trust is accumulated at the individual level and must be rebuilt when individuals change.
questions_to_ask: If the primary MOTM contact at this client left tomorrow, how much of the trust in the relationship is in the institution versus the individual?
Am I building genuine personal trust with this client — or am I relying on MOTM's credibility to do the work?
What is my own personal relationship with this client, independent of my role at MOTM?
recommended_action: Invest in building personal trust independently of MOTM's institutional credibility. This means showing genuine personal curiosity about the client's situation, remembering personal details and following up on them, being willing to have conversations that are not directly about MOTM's services, and taking personal positions on questions where many advisors would be evasive. The goal is for the client to trust this specific person — who happens to work at MOTM.
what_not_to_do: Do not rely on MOTM's brand, methodology, or case studies as the primary trust-building tools. Do not treat client relationships as transferable assets of MOTM — they are personal assets that happen to be associated with MOTM. Do not underestimate the trust damage caused by changing the person who has the primary client relationship without a carefully managed transition.
motm_application: A MOTM prospect who is impressed by MOTM's process and track record but has never had a genuinely personal conversation with anyone at MOTM will not feel the level of trust that produces long-term engagement. The BD person who asks about the MD's personal business history, who remembers what the MD said about a specific challenge three months ago, who expresses a genuine personal view on a commercial question — is building the kind of trust that no presentation deck can replace.

principle_name: The Quick-Impact Trust Actions — What to Do Right Now to Begin Building Trust
author: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford
chapter: Chapter 22 — The Quick-Impact List to Gain Trust
when_to_use: As a practical action guide for any MOTM BD person who wants to immediately improve the trust level in a specific client or prospect relationship. These are actions that can be taken in the next meeting or interaction.
when_not_to_use: These actions are not tricks or techniques to be deployed selectively. They only work when they are consistent with a genuine orientation toward the client's interests. Isolated tactics without a sincere foundation will be detected and will damage trust.
principle: There are specific actions that reliably build trust quickly when they are sincere. Among the most powerful: Demonstrate interest in the client as a person, not just as a client. Say what you think, even when it is uncomfortable. Show that you will speak truth whether it helps or hurts MOTM's commercial interests. Ask great questions and listen to the answers. Remember what the client told you in past conversations. Follow up on small commitments perfectly. Be consistent — do what you say, say what you mean, every time. Be willing to say I don't know. Be on the client's side even when it costs MOTM something. Never name-drop or self-promote. And most powerfully: demonstrate that you are more interested in their success than in MOTM's success.
questions_to_ask: What small commitment can I make and deliver perfectly before our next interaction?
Is there something this client told me that I can follow up on — something that demonstrates I was genuinely listening?
What is the one thing I can do in the next interaction that would visibly demonstrate I am on this client's side rather than on MOTM's side?
recommended_action: After every MOTM client meeting, identify three specific follow-up actions: one small commitment that can be delivered by the next day, one thing to remember and follow up on from the conversation, and one way to demonstrate genuine interest in the client as a person. Execute all three without exception.
what_not_to_do: Do not make small commitments that you will not keep — they destroy reliability. Do not treat follow-up as optional or informal — it is the most reliable trust-building activity available. Do not focus all trust-building effort on large gestures while neglecting the small, consistent actions that actually define reliability in the client's experience.
motm_application: Practical immediate trust actions for MOTM BD: (1) Send a one-paragraph note after every client meeting summarising what was discussed and what MOTM will do next — this alone dramatically improves perceived reliability. (2) Call a client when you find something useful to them, even when there is no commercial reason to call. (3) If you cannot deliver something on time, tell the client before the deadline, not after. (4) When a client asks for something MOTM cannot do well, say so directly rather than trying to fit it into MOTM's service model. (5) Remember personal details and follow up on them — if a client mentioned a family event or a business challenge, ask about it next time. These five actions, done consistently, build more trust than any capability presentation.
